deck: 20 Head First Java::06 Using the Java Library

cards.front: Why choose an ArrayList over an array when the number of elements changes?
cards.back: An ArrayList resizes itself; an array's length is fixed at creation
cards.extra: You can add and remove without allocating and copying by hand. The cost is a wrapper around an array plus boxing for primitives — worth it unless you are measuring.

cards.front: How do you put an element in and take one out of an ArrayList?
cards.extra: Both are methods, which is the whole difference from an array. Removing shifts the later elements down, so it is O(n) — not free.

cards.back: No — it holds objects; primitives are autoboxed into wrappers
cards.extra: ArrayList<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>(); nums.add(3); boxes 3 into an Integer, and unboxes on the way out. Since Java 5 that happens automatically.
It does not throw. That is why one call can both test membership and find the position: if (i >= 0) means present at i. The signature alone does not tell you this — the API docs do.

cards.front: Why can an array of primitives be faster than an ArrayList of the same numbers?
cards.back: No boxing/unboxing and no method call per access
cards.extra: Each element in an ArrayList<Integer> is a separate heap object, so a loop creates or dereferences wrappers. For hot numeric loops an int[] wins.

cards.front: What is the point of reading the API docs for a method you already know the name of?
cards.back: The edge-case behaviour — what happens on empty, missing or null input
cards.extra: A signature says int indexOf(Object); only the prose says it returns -1 when absent. Guessing here produces null checks and try/catch that were never needed.
Since Java 9 the JDK is split into modules, and everything this book has used so far lives in java.base. That is why no import of the module is ever needed.

cards.front: What does && give you that & does not?
cards.back: Short-circuiting: the right side is not evaluated when the left is false
cards.extra: if (ref != null && ref.size > 0) is safe; with & both sides always run and the null check is useless. Same idea for || versus |.

cards.front: Why does the book split a class into many small methods instead of one big one?
cards.back: Smaller units are easier to test, debug and change
cards.extra: Each method has one job, so a failure localises. The game class splits "play" into two methods purely for that reason, not for reuse.

cards.front: Why is a plain array awkward when the list must grow?
cards.back: Its length is fixed: you must track the next free slot and copy into a bigger array
cards.extra: The book's three "options" are all variations of tracking an index and doubling manually. ArrayList exists so that bookkeeping is the library's job, not yours.

cards.front: What does ArrayList add that an array cannot do at all?
cards.back: Remove and insert in the middle, with the size adjusting itself
cards.extra: remove(i) shifts everything after i down and shrinks the size. An array cannot change length, so the last slot stays whatever it was.

cards.front: You replace an int[] field with ArrayList<Integer>. What else must change?
cards.back: The loops: length becomes size(), and elements are objects, not ints
cards.extra: for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++), or an enhanced for. Indexing still works, but list[i] is list.get(i).

cards.front: What does || do when the left side is already true?
cards.back: Skips the right side entirely and yields true
cards.extra: Short-circuit evaluation. That is why if (o == null || o.isEmpty()) is safe and the mirror image with | throws.

cards.front: What is the fastest way to find out what a library class can do?
cards.back: Read its page in the API documentation
cards.extra: The docs list every method, its parameters, its return value and the exceptions it throws. Guessing from the class name costs more time than one lookup.
